analysis.one_liner: Ends cash bail in federal criminal cases and cuts federal grants to states that keep it.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in a House Judiciary subcommittee with 39 Democratic sponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop federal judges from requiring people accused of crimes to pay money to stay out of jail before trial. It would also make any state that still uses cash bail ineligible for federal Justice Department grants under the Edward Byrne program, with that money redirected to states that have ended the practice. The goal is that whether someone waits at home or in jail before trial depends on risk, not ability to pay.
analysis.who_benefits: Poor and low-income people accused of crimes who currently sit in jail before trial because they cannot afford bail. The bill's own findings say nearly 60% of jail inmates are unconvicted pretrial detainees and that people with money can buy their freedom while poor defendants stay locked up [S3]. It would also ease the roughly $14 billion annual cost of pretrial detention borne by state and local taxpayers [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Unconvicted defendants who can't afford bail

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any federal judge from using payment of money as a condition of pretrial release in any criminal case in federal courts, so federal pretrial release would depend on court appearance and public safety risk instead of cash [S3].

Makes states that use cash bail ineligible for Byrne JAG grant funding beginning the third fiscal year after enactment, and requires the Attorney General to redistribute those funds among eligible states, giving states a financial reason to replace cash bail [S2] [S3].

The bill's findings cite that nearly 60% of jail inmates are unconvicted pretrial detainees, about 75% of them charged with nonviolent crimes, and that pretrial detention costs state and local governments an estimated $14 billion a year [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The commercial bail bond industry, which charges defendants fees to post bond, would lose its federal-system market and face pressure in states. State and local governments that keep cash bail would lose federal JAG public-safety grant money, meaning fewer federal dollars for local law enforcement programs until they change their systems [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Bail bond companies and noncompliant state governments

drawbacks.text: The federal ban is largely symbolic: federal courts already operate under a pretrial release system based on risk rather than a commercial bail market, so the everyday harm the bill targets happens in state courts, which the bill reaches only indirectly through the grant penalty [S3].

States that keep cash bail would lose Byrne JAG public-safety funding, and the bill requires that money to be reallocated to other states, so local law enforcement programs in noncompliant states would pay a price even if their legislators never chose the bail system [S2] [S3].

Replacing cash bail with risk-based release raises the opposite risk that people judged risky are held without any money-based path to release, an objection raised in bail-reform debates generally; the bill text does not include limits on preventive detention [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change would help a large group — hundreds of thousands of unconvicted people jailed each year mainly because they are poor — and reduce billions in detention costs, while the main costs fall on the bail bond industry and on states that refuse to change. The design is uneven: the direct federal ban affects a small share of the problem because cash bail is mostly a state and local practice, so the real mechanism is the grant cutoff, which works slowly and punishes local programs rather than defendants.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its Crime subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Lieu introduced the No Money Bail Act on March 8, 2017 with 38 cosponsors, all Democrats [S1] [S4].

The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction, and on March 17, 2017 to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations; no further action appears in the record for the rest of the 115th Congress [S5].
The bill never received a committee vote, a markup, or a floor vote in either chamber before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The commercial bail bond industry and cash-bail systems are untouched: no state lost grant money and no defendant's bail situation changed, while poor defendants continue to face pretrial detention based on ability to pay.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The bail bond industry and cash-bail status quo

for.name: Rep. Ted Lieu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to end cash bail in federal cases and condition state grant eligibility on ending cash bail.

for.name: 38 House cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors including Reps. Cummings, Nadler, Ellison, and Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all were Democrats and none of it advanced past referral.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee chair and subcommittee leadership with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill stayed in the Crime subcommittee from March 2017 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Commercial bail bond industry
against.role: Bail bond agents and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Actively opposed cash-bail-reform legislation at the state and federal level during this period, arguing it releases dangerous defendants and eliminates a constitutionally grounded service.

sides.party_line_note: All 38 cosponsors were Democrats with no Republican support recorded, and the Republican-led Judiciary Committee never moved the bill [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The industry sells a service — paying a defendant's bond for a fee — that exists only because cash bail exists; ending cash bail in federal cases and financially pressuring states to end it removes its market. Its fees fall hardest on the same poor defendants the bill tries to protect.

industries.industry: State and local governments with cash bail systems
industries.note: Noncompliant states would lose Byrne JAG public-safety grant money until they end cash bail, a real fiscal cost to local programs. The bill's findings note pretrial detention already costs state and local governments an estimated $14 billion a year, so ending cash bail could also save them money [S3].

industries.industry: County and local jails and detention services
industries.note: Jails profit from housing pretrial detainees; ending cash bail would reduce their unconvicted populations and the revenue tied to them, while shifting some spending to risk-assessment and supervision services.
